If used, such therapy should be limit- ed to 1 or 2 weeks; there has also been some concern about the presence of these drugs in breast milk.5,6 The efficacy of metoclopramide in stimulating lactation in women with preterm deliveries has been questioned by a controlled study.7 Domperidone has also been reported to increase milk production,6,8 and may cause fewer adverse central effects than metoclopramide. Nevertheless, the FDA has warned against the use of domperidone because of the po- tential risks of adverse effects in both mother and infant.9 Protirelin has been given intranasally to stimulate lactation by increasing serum prolactin concentrations, but is expen- sive, and a suitable commercial preparation is unavaila- ble.5 Although oxytocin nasal spray has been tried to pro- mote milk ejection, a double-blind, placebo-controlled study10 of women expressing milk for preterm infants found that although milk production increased marginally in the first 2 days with oxytocin, there was no difference overall after 5 days. Most mothers also believed that they were receiving the active spray suggesting a significant placebo effect.
